title: The Story of Sir Pellias: Chapter 4
paragraphs: _How Queen Guinevere quarreled with Sir Gawaine, and how Sir Gawaine left the court of King Arthur for a while._

Queen Guinevere held Sir Pellias in high regard, and in just the same measure she disliked Sir Gawaine. Many people said Sir Gawaine had a silver tongue, and at times he could talk so well that he won others over to his wishes. But he was proud, stern, and haughty. So he did not always accept it when the Lady Guinevere ordered him about as she did the other knights of that court. She also could never forget how Sir Gawaine had refused her at Cameliard, when she begged him and his companions for help in her time of trouble. Nor could she forget how rudely he had spoken to her then. So there was little affection between these two proud people. Queen Guinevere held to her own way, and Sir Gawaine held to his, whatever happened.

One day Sir Gawaine, Sir Griflet, and Sir Constantine of Cornwall sat talking with five ladies of the Queen’s court. They were in a garden of woven branches that lay beneath the tower of the Lady Guinevere, and their talk was very pleasant. At times they told jokes and tales and made merry. At other times one of them would take up a lute they had brought with them, and play it and sing.

While these lords and ladies sat enjoying their conversation and songs, Queen Guinevere sat at a window that looked out over the garden. The window was not very high above the ground, so she could hear everything they said. But the lords and ladies had no idea that the Queen could hear them, so they talked and laughed very freely. The Queen greatly enjoyed their talk and the music they made.

That day was unusually mild, and it was well into the late afternoon. The lords and ladies were dressed in very bright clothes, and Sir Gawaine was the most brightly dressed of them all. He wore sky-blue silk embroidered with silver thread. He was playing the lute and singing a ballad in a most pleasing voice. Queen Guinevere sat beside the open window and was very glad to listen to him.

Queen Guinevere had a greyhound of which she was wonderfully fond. She was so fond of it that she had dressed its neck with a gold collar set with red jewels. At that moment the hound came running into the garden, and its feet were wet and muddy. When it heard Sir Gawaine singing and playing the lute, it ran to him and jumped up on him. Sir Gawaine was very angry at this. He clenched his fist and struck the hound on the head with his knuckles, and the hound cried out loudly.

When Queen Guinevere saw that blow, she was greatly offended. She called out from her window, “Why do you strike my dog, Messire?” The lords and ladies in the garden were very surprised. They were deeply embarrassed to find that the Queen had been so close by, and had heard everything they said and seen everything they did.
But Sir Gawaine answered boldly, “Your dog insulted me, Lady, and whoever insults me, I strike.”
Then Queen Guinevere grew very angry with Sir Gawaine. She said, “Your speech is too bold, Messire.” And Sir Gawaine said, “Not too bold, Lady, but only bold enough to defend my rights.”

At this the Lady Guinevere’s face burned like fire, and her eyes shone very bright. She said, “I am sure you have forgotten whom you are speaking to, Sir Knight.” At that, Sir Gawaine smiled bitterly and said, “And you, Lady, do not remember that I am the son of a king so powerful that he needs no help from any other king to defend his rights.”

At these words everyone there fell as silent as if they had been turned to stone, for that speech was extremely bold and proud. They all looked at the ground, for they did not dare to look at Queen Guinevere or at Sir Gawaine. The Lady Guinevere was also silent for a long time, trying to recover from what he had said. When she spoke, it was as though her anger half choked her. She said, “Sir Knight, you are proud and arrogant beyond measure. I have never heard of anyone who dared to answer his Queen as you have spoken to me. But this is my court, and I may command in it as I choose. So I now order you to leave, and to show your face no more, either here or in the Hall or in any place where I hold my court. You are an offense to me, and in none of these places will you be allowed to show your face until you ask my pardon for the insult you have given me.” Then Sir Gawaine stood up and bowed very low to Queen Guinevere, and he said, “Lady, I go. And I will not come back until you are willing to tell me that you are sorry for the rude way you have treated me, now and at other times in front of my peers.”

With these words Sir Gawaine left that place, and he did not turn his head to look back. Queen Guinevere went into her chamber and wept in secret, out of anger and shame. She was truly grieved at what had happened. Yet she was so proud that she would not have taken back the words she had spoken, even if she could have.

When the news of that quarrel had gone around the castle, it reached the ears of Sir Ewaine. He went straight to Sir Gawaine and asked what had happened. Sir Gawaine, who was like a man out of his mind and in deep despair, told him everything. Then Sir Ewaine said, “You were certainly wrong to speak to the Queen as you did. Still, if you are banished from this court, I will go with you, for you are my first cousin and my companion, and my heart is bound to you.” So Sir Ewaine went to King Arthur and said, “Lord, my cousin, Sir Gawaine, has been banished from this court by the Queen. I cannot say he has not earned that punishment, but I would gladly ask your leave to go with him.”

King Arthur was very sad at this, but he kept a steady face. He said, “Messire, I will not stop you from going where you wish. As for your kinsman, I suppose he gave the Queen such great offense that she could not do otherwise.”

So Sir Ewaine and Sir Gawaine both went to their lodgings and ordered their squires to help them put on their armor. Then they and their squires rode out of Camelot and took the road toward the forest lands.

The two knights and their squires traveled all that day until the gray of evening, when the birds were singing their last songs before closing their eyes for the night. As evening came quickly on, the knights feared they would not find friendly lodging before dark, and they spoke about this a good deal. But when they reached the top of a certain hill, they saw below them a valley, very fair and well farmed, with many cottages and small farms. In the middle of the valley stood a fine abbey, very beautiful to look at. Sir Gawaine said to Sir Ewaine, “If that abbey is a house of monks, I believe we will find excellent lodging there tonight.”
So they rode down into the valley to the abbey. At the small gate they found a porter, and from him they learned that it was indeed an abbey of monks. They were very glad and rejoiced greatly.

When the abbot of that abbey learned who they were and what high rank they held, he was delighted to welcome them. He brought them to the part of the abbey where he himself lived. There he bade them welcome and had a good supper set before them, and they were very glad of it. The abbot was cheerful and loved to talk with strangers. So he asked the two knights eagerly why they were wandering as knights-errant. But they told him nothing about the quarrel at court, only that they were looking for adventure. At this the abbot said, “Ha, Messires, if you are looking for adventures, you may find one not far from here.”

Sir Gawaine said, “What adventure is that?” And the abbot answered, “I will tell you. If you travel east from here, after a while you will come to a very fair castle of gray stone. In front of that castle you will find a good level meadow, and in the middle of the meadow a sycamore tree. On the tree hangs a shield, which certain ladies insult in a very strange way. If you forbid those ladies to insult that shield, you will find a very good adventure.”
Then Sir Gawaine said, “That is a very strange matter. Tomorrow morning we will go to that place and try to find out what sort of adventure it is.” And the abbot said, “Do so,” and laughed heartily.

When the next morning came, Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine said farewell to the abbot and left that place, riding east as the abbot had advised. After they had ridden that way for two or three hours or more, they saw ahead of them the edge of a forest, green and shady with leaves, and very cheerful in the warmth of the early summer day. And behold! Right at the edge of the woods stood a fair, strong castle of gray stone, with glass windows shining brightly against the sky.

Then Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine saw that everything was just as the abbot had said. In front of the castle was a smooth, level meadow with a sycamore tree in the middle of it. As they drew near, they saw that a black shield hung in the branches of the tree. Soon they could see that it bore the badge of three white goshawks with spread wings. But the most extraordinary thing was that in front of that shield stood seven young damsels, very fair of face, and they kept heaping insults on the shield. Some of the damsels struck it again and again with peeled willow rods, and others threw lumps of clay at it, so that the shield was badly spoiled. Close to the shield was a noble-looking knight dressed all in black armor and seated on a black war-horse. It was plain that the shield belonged to that knight, for he carried no other. Yet although it was very likely his own shield, the knight made no protest, by word or by action, to stop the damsels from insulting it.

Then Sir Ewaine said to Sir Gawaine, “That is a very strange thing I see over there. Perhaps one of us is meant to fight that knight.” And Sir Gawaine said, “Perhaps so.” Then Sir Ewaine said, “If so, then I will take the adventure.” “Not so,” said Sir Gawaine, “for I will take it myself. I am the elder of us two, and more experienced in knighthood.” So Sir Ewaine said, “Very well. Let it be that way, for you are a much more powerful knight than I, and it would be a pity if one of us failed in this task.” Then Sir Gawaine said, “So be it, and I will take it.”

He set spurs to his horse and rode quickly to where the damsels were insulting the black shield. He set his spear in position and shouted in a loud voice, “Get away! Get away!” When the damsels saw the armed knight riding at them like that, they fled from him, shrieking.

Then the Sable Knight, who had been sitting a short way off, rode forward in a very stately manner to Sir Gawaine. He said, “Sir Knight, why do you interfere with those ladies?” Sir Gawaine replied, “Because they were insulting what seemed to me a noble and knightly shield.” At this the Sable Knight spoke very proudly, saying, “Sir Knight, that shield belongs to me, and I assure you I am quite able to take care of it without the interference of any other defender.” To this Sir Gawaine said, “It does not seem so, Sir Knight.”

Then the Sable Knight said, “Messire, if you think you can take better care of that shield than I can, I think you would do well to prove your words with your body.” To this Sir Gawaine said, “I will do my best to show you that I am better able to guard that shield than you, who own it.”

At this the Sable Knight, without further talk, rode to the sycamore tree and took down the shield that hung there. He fitted the shield to his arm, took his spear in hand, and made himself ready for defense. Sir Gawaine also made himself ready, and then each knight took whatever place on the field seemed fitting to him.

When the people of that castle saw that a fight with weapons was about to begin, they crowded in great numbers onto the walls. There were as many as forty ladies, squires, and people of different ranks looking down on the field of battle from the walls.

When the knights were fully ready, Sir Ewaine gave the signal for the charge. Each knight shouted aloud, drove his spurs into his war-horse, and rushed forward to the attack with a noise as loud as thunder.

Sir Gawaine thought he would easily defeat his opponent in this charge, and that he could throw him from the saddle without much trouble. Hardly any knight in that realm was equal to Sir Gawaine in strength and skill. Indeed, he had never yet been knocked from his horse in combat, except by King Arthur. So when the two rode at each other, Sir Gawaine was certain that his opponent would fall before him. But it was not so. In that charge Sir Gawaine’s spear broke into many pieces, but the spear of the Sable Knight held firm. Sir Gawaine was thrown violently out of the saddle and struck the dust with a terrible crash. He was so astonished by the fall that it seemed to him not that he had fallen from his saddle, but that the earth had risen up and struck him. He lay there for a while, stunned by the blow and by his astonishment.

But when he heard the shouts of the people on the castle wall, he quickly got up from the dust. He was so filled with rage and shame that he seemed like a man gone wild. He drew his sword and rushed furiously at his enemy, meaning to cut him down by sheer strength. The other knight, seeing him come at him like this, at once leaped from his own saddle, drew his sword, and set himself ready either to attack or to defend. They lashed at each other, wheeling this way and that, and struck with such fury that the blows were terrible to watch. When Sir Ewaine saw how fierce the fight was, he set spurs to his horse and pushed it between the two fighting knights. He cried out loudly, “Sir Knights! Sir Knights! What is this? There is no cause here for such a desperate battle.” But Sir Gawaine cried out furiously, “Let be! Let be! Stand aside! This quarrel is no business of yours.” And the Sable Knight said, “On horseback or on foot, I am ready to meet that knight at any time.”

But Sir Ewaine said, “Not so. You will fight no more in this quarrel. Shame on you, Gawaine! Shame on you for seeking such a desperate quarrel with a knight who only met you in a friendly way, in a fair contest!”

Then Sir Gawaine saw that Sir Ewaine was completely fair and right. So he put his sword away without a word, though he was close to tears at the shame of his defeat. The Sable Knight put his sword away too, and so peace was made between the two.

Then the Sable Knight said, “I am glad this quarrel is over. I can see, Messires, that you are knights of great nobility and fine breeding. So I would like us to be friends and companions from now on, not enemies. I beg you to come with me a short way from here, where I have set up my lodging. There we can rest and refresh ourselves in my pavilion.”
To this Sir Ewaine said, “I thank you for your courtesy, Sir Knight, and we will gladly go with you.” And Sir Gawaine said, “I agree.” So the three knights left the field of battle at once.

When they came to the edge of the forest, Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine saw a very fine pavilion of green silk set up beneath a tree. Around the pavilion were many attendants of all kinds, dressed in green and white. Sir Gawaine saw from this that the knight who had overthrown him must surely be a man of very high rank, and this comforted him greatly. Then the esquires of the three knights came and took off the helmets, each esquire for his own knight, so that the knights could be comfortable. When this was done, Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine saw that the Sable Knight had a very handsome face. It was ruddy, and his hair was as red as copper. Then Sir Ewaine said to him, “Sir Unknown Knight, my companion here is Sir Gawaine, son of King Urien of Gore, and I am Ewaine, the son of King Lot of Orkney. Now I ask you, in the same way, to tell us who you are.”
“Ha,” said the other, “I am glad you are such famous and royal knights, for I am also of royal blood. I am Sir Marhaus, the son of the King of Ireland.”

Sir Gawaine was very glad to learn how high in rank the knight was who had overthrown him. He said to Sir Marhaus, “Messire, I swear that you are one of the most terrible knights in the world. Today you have done to me what only one other knight in all the world has ever done, and that is King Arthur, who is my uncle and my lord. Now you must certainly come to the Court of King Arthur. He will be wonderfully glad to see you, and perhaps he will make you a Knight of his Round Table—and there is no honor in all the world that is so great.” He spoke without thinking, and then he remembered. He struck his fist against his forehead and cried out, “Aha! Aha! Who am I to invite you to the Court of King Arthur, when only yesterday I was disgraced and banished from it?”

Then Sir Marhaus felt very sorry for Sir Gawaine, and he asked about the trouble that weighed on him. Sir Ewaine told Sir Marhaus all about the quarrel, and at this Sir Marhaus felt even sorrier for Sir Gawaine. He said, “Messires, I like you both very much, and I would gladly join you as a companion in the adventures you are about to undertake. For now I need not stay here any longer. You must know that I was bound to defend those ladies who attacked my shield, until I had overthrown seven knights on their behalf. I must tell you that Sir Gawaine was the seventh knight I have overthrown. Now that I have overthrown him, I am released from my duty and may go with you.”

Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine were astonished that any knight should be under so strange a duty as to defend those who attacked his shield. They begged Sir Marhaus to tell them why he had been bound to such a pledge. So Sir Marhaus said, “I will tell you. This is how it happened. Some time ago I was traveling in these parts with a hawk on my wrist. I was dressed very lightly, in holiday clothes. I wore a tunic of green silk and hose, one leg green and one white. I had nothing to defend myself with but a light shield and a short sword. I came to a stream of water, very deep and swift, and I saw before me a stone bridge crossing it. The bridge was so narrow that only one horseman could cross at a time. So I rode onto the bridge, and I was partway across when I saw a knight in armor coming the other way. Behind the knight, on a pillion seat, sat a very fair lady with golden hair and a very proud manner. When that knight saw me on the bridge, he cried out, ‘Get back! Get back, and let me pass!’ But I would not do this. I said, ‘Not so, Sir Knight. I have come so far onto this bridge that I surely have the right of way to finish crossing, and it is for you to wait and let me cross.’ But the knight would not do so. He at once got ready to fight and came against me on the bridge, meaning either to kill me or to drive me back to the other end. But he could not do this, for I defended myself very well with my light weapons. I pushed my horse against his horse and drove him backward off the bridge and into the water. The horse, the knight, and the lady all fell into it together with a terrible uproar.

“At this the lady shrieked loudly, and both she and the knight were close to drowning. The knight was dressed completely in armor, so he could not lift himself above the water. Seeing their danger, I leaped from my horse into the water. With great effort, and at great risk to myself, I was able to bring them both to the shore.

“But that lady was very offended with me, for her fine clothes were wet through and spoiled by the water, and she scolded me fiercely. I knelt down before her and begged her pardon with all humility, but she kept on scolding me. Then I offered to do any penance she might set for me. At this the lady seemed to soften, for she said, ‘Very well, I will set you a penance.’ When her knight had recovered, she said, ‘Come with us.’ So I mounted my horse and followed them. After we had gone a long way, we came to this place, and here she gave me her command. ‘Sir Knight,’ she said, ‘this castle belongs to me and to this knight, who is my lord. This shall be your penance for the insult you have given me. You shall take your shield and hang it in that sycamore tree over there. Every day I will send some of my own damsels out from the castle, and they shall insult that shield. You shall not only put up with whatever insult they offer, but you shall defend them against all comers, until you have overcome seven knights.’
“So I have done until this morning, when you, Sir Gawaine, came here. You are the seventh knight I have fought, and since I have overcome you, my penance is now ended and I am free.”

Then Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine told Sir Marhaus how glad they were that his penance was complete, and all three were very well pleased with one another. Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine stayed that night in the pavilion of Sir Marhaus. The next morning they got up, washed themselves in a forest stream, and left that place.
So they entered the forest once more and made their way along certain paths, not knowing where they led. They traveled all that morning and until the afternoon came.

As they traveled, Sir Marhaus said suddenly, “Messires, do you know where we have come to?” “No,” they said, “we do not.” Then Sir Marhaus said, “This part of the forest is called Arroy, and it is also called ‘The Forest of Adventure.’ It is well known that when a knight, or a party of knights, enters this forest, they will surely meet with some sort of adventure. Some come out of it with honor, and others fail.” And Sir Ewaine said, “I am glad we have come here. Now let us go forward into this forest.”

So the three knights and their esquires went on through that woodland, where the silence was so deep that the tread of their horses on the ground was hardly heard. There was no song of any bird and no sound of any voice, and hardly any light reached into the gloom of that wood. The knights said to one another, “This is truly a very strange place, and perhaps a place of enchantment.”

When they had come into the very middle of these dark woods, they suddenly saw a fawn as white as milk on the path before them. Around the fawn’s neck was a collar of pure gold. The fawn stood and looked at them, but when they came near, it turned and ran along a very narrow path. Then Sir Gawaine said, “Let us follow that fawn and see where it goes.” And the others said, “Agreed.” So they followed the narrow path until they suddenly came to a little open lawn, bright with sunlight. In the middle of the lawn was a fountain of water. There was no fawn to be seen, but, behold, beside the fountain sat a wonderfully beautiful lady, dressed all in green. The lady was combing her hair with a golden comb, and her hair was as black as a raven’s wing. On her arms she wore marvelous bracelets of emeralds and opal stones set in finely worked gold. Her face was as white as ivory, and her eyes were as bright as jewels set in ivory. When the lady saw the knights, she stood up and laid aside her golden comb. She tied up the locks of her hair with ribbons of scarlet silk, and then she came to the knights and greeted them.

Then the three knights got down from their horses at once, and Sir Gawaine said, “Lady, I believe you are not of mortal kind, but of the fairy folk.” To this the lady said, “Sir Gawaine, you are right.” Sir Gawaine wondered that she knew his name so well. Then he said to her, “Lady, who are you?” and she answered, “My name is Nymue, and I am the chief of those Ladies of the Lake of whom you may have heard. It was I who gave King Arthur his sword Excalibur, for I am very friendly to King Arthur and to all the noble Knights of his Court. That is why I know you all. And I know that you, Sir Marhaus, will become one of the most famous Knights of the Round Table.” All three wondered at the lady’s words. Then she said, “Please tell me, what is it you seek in these parts?” And they said, “We seek adventure.” “Well,” she said, “I will lead you to an adventure, but it is Sir Gawaine who must take it on.” And Sir Gawaine said, “That is very glad news.” Then the lady said, “Take me up behind you on your saddle, Sir Gawaine, and I will show you that adventure.” So Sir Gawaine took the lady up behind him on the saddle, and behold, she brought with her a fragrance such as he had never known before. It was so delicate that it seemed to Sir Gawaine that the forest itself gave off the perfume the Lady of the Lake brought with her.

So the Lady of the Lake led them by many winding ways out of that part of the forest. She led them along various roads and paths until they came out into an open country, rich and pleasant to look at. She led them up a very high hill, and from the top they looked down on a fertile, level plain, like a table spread out before them. In the middle of the plain they saw a noble castle built all of red stone and red bricks. Beside it was a small town, also built of red bricks.

As they sat on their horses at the top of the hill, they suddenly saw a knight in red armor come out from a grove of trees. They saw him ride about the meadow in front of the castle, and they saw him challenge those inside the castle. Then the drawbridge of the castle was suddenly let down, and ten knights in full armor came out. They saw those ten knights attack the one knight in red armor, and they saw the one knight attack the ten. For a while the ten held out against the one, but he attacked them so fiercely that he struck down four of them very quickly. Then the rest broke and fled from him, and the Red Knight chased them about the meadow with great fury. They saw him strike one man out of his saddle, and then another, and another, until only two of the knights were left.
Sir Gawaine said, “What a wonderful thing to watch!” But the Lady of the Lake only smiled. “Wait a little longer,” she said.

So they waited, and they saw that the Red Knight struck down all his enemies except those two. When he had put those two in great danger of their lives, he suddenly sheathed his sword and gave himself up to them. They saw the two knights bring the Red Knight to the castle, and when they had brought him there, a lady on the castle wall shouted at him with great violence of language. They saw the two knights take the Red Knight and tie his hands behind his back. They tied his feet beneath his horse’s belly, and they drove him away from that place.

They saw all this from the top of that hill, and the Lady of the Lake said to Sir Gawaine, “There you will find your adventure, Sir Gawaine.” And Sir Gawaine said, “I will go,” and the Lady of the Lake said, “Do so.”
Then, behold, she vanished from their sight, and they were greatly amazed.
